question_text: According to the course material, a depreciable asset is a non-current asset whose value likely diminishes with usage or over time; examples are building, machinery, equipment, motor vehicle; a typical non-depreciable asset is:
explanation: Land is a typical non-depreciable asset.

question_text: According to the course material, if cost of land and building is N10.5 million where land is N2 million, the value of the depreciable asset will be:
explanation: Only the building N8.5 million is depreciated.

question_text: According to the course material, depreciation in accounting is only a cost allocation process; it is a misconception that depreciation is:
option_a: the money set aside for the replacement of a non-current asset
explanation: Ordinary depreciation is not a replacement fund.

question_text: According to the course material, where an entity utilises depreciation as a means to set aside money to specifically replace an asset, such process is called:
explanation: Funded depreciation is a financing function.

question_text: According to the course material, methods of depreciation include straight-line, reducing balance, sum of the years' digit, unit of production, and:
explanation: Methods include machine hours.

question_text: According to the course material, useful life is the period of time the non-current asset is expected to generate benefit; the physical life of the asset may not necessarily coincide with:
option_a: the estimated useful life for the purpose of depreciation
explanation: Physical life may exceed estimated useful life.

question_text: According to the course material, cost of plant and machinery includes purchase price, freight and its associated insurance, installation cost, and:
explanation: Cost includes incidental costs to bring the asset into use.

question_text: According to the course material, Look-and-See Ventures acquired machinery list price N50,000 for N40,000 plus installation N2,000, legal fees N1,000, freight N500; the cost of the machinery is:
explanation: Use actual price N40,000 plus incidentals = N43,500.

question_text: According to the course material, salvage value also known as scrap value or residual value is the amount the non-current asset will realise:
explanation: Residual/scrap/salvage value is realisable after useful life.

explanation: WDV = cost minus accumulated depreciation.

question_text: According to the course material, the unit of production method allocates depreciable value based on the number of outputs produced; if machinery costs N100,000, scrap N10,000, capacity 500,000 units, depreciation for 40,000 units is based on:
option_a: depreciable value allocated by units produced in the period
explanation: Unit of production uses output of the period.

question_text: According to the course material, the revaluation method values the non-current asset at beginning and end of a period; the difference represents depreciation and is appropriate for a group of assets such as:
explanation: Revaluation method suits loose tools, crates, containers.

explanation: Depreciation is not credited to the asset a/c.

question_text: According to the course material, amortisation is similar to depreciation as it is to intangible assets as depreciation is to:
explanation: Amortisation allocates cost of intangibles.

question_text: According to the course material, what constitutes a non-current asset to a firm depends on what it does with that asset; a transport company treats motor vehicles as non-current assets, whereas a vehicle dealer treats similar motor vehicles as:
explanation: A dealer holds vehicles as inventories.

question_text: According to the course material, non-current assets acquired are treated as capital expenditure because the assets generate benefits in:
explanation: NCA benefits more than one period.

question_text: According to the course material, inventories are generally the unsold portion of goods held for resale; what constitutes inventories depends on:
option_a: the nature of the business of an entity
explanation: Inventory classification depends on the nature of the business.

question_text: According to the course material, generally inventories are valued at lower of cost and:
explanation: Lower of cost and NRV/fair value.

question_text: According to the course material, common methods of valuing inventory are First In First Out (FIFO), Last In First Out (LIFO), Average (simple and weighted) and methods determined by:
explanation: Accounting policy determines the method.

question_text: According to the course material, a periodic inventory valuation occurs where an entity takes inventory count and determines the value at the end of the accounting year; it will be unable to determine closing inventory and cost of sales until:
explanation: Periodic model waits for stock-taking.

question_text: According to the course material, perpetual inventory approach maintains inventory records on a continuous basis whenever there is movement whether through purchases or sales; the entity can ascertain closing inventory:
explanation: Perpetual records are updated after each purchase or sale.

question_text: According to the course material, the physical count at year end under perpetual inventory is to verify correspondence of the number of inventory based on physical count and:
explanation: Year-end count verifies records vs physical stock.

question_text: According to the course material, whichever inventory system is adopted, the entity basically uses any of FIFO, LIFO, SAM and:
explanation: SAM and WAM are simple and weighted average methods.
